title: Notion Pricing 2026: Plans, AI and What Each Costs
summary: Notion pricing breaks down into Free, Plus, Business, and Enterprise plans. Understand the actual cost of each tier to make your purchase decision.
body_markdown:
## Notion automation limits and where Activepieces fits


If a team only needs cross-app workflows, it has no reason to move up a Notion tier for them: the Activepieces pricing page lists **unlimited flows on every plan** from Free through Ultimate, so the number of flows is never what you pay for; the meter is credits, and a run is 1 credit however many steps it has, whereas Zapier's pricing page bills a task per action and Make's a credit per module.


### What Notion's built-in automations cover


Inside the database they live in, Notion's native automations act: a page is added, a property changes, and Notion edits another property, creates a page, or sends a notification.


If your process stays inside Notion, use them. Paying for a second tool to do what a built-in trigger already does is waste, and you add a failure point for nothing.


When the work touches a system Notion doesn't own, the limits show up.


> Paying for a second tool to do what a built-in trigger already does is waste, and you add a failure point for nothing.


When a support ticket arrives in a CRM, someone needs a categorized summary in a chat channel. When a status flips to "Blocked", the team should hear about it somewhere other than a database view.


Those cases are where teams start reading the pricing page for a higher plan, and where the upgrade may be solving the wrong problem.


### Connecting Notion to other apps


Through its Notion connector, Activepieces, an AI automation platform, can take a Notion event as a trigger or an action alongside other apps.


Two patterns cover most of what teams ask for: a form submission becomes a new database row, and a status change becomes a Slack message to the right channel.


The connector is one of the 746 integrations in the open source monorepo, about 60% of them community-contributed, under an MIT-licensed core, so its source sits in the` packages/pieces/community` directory on GitHub.


Here is the shape of the flow. It starts with a HubSpot trigger for a new ticket, passes the content through two AI steps that rewrite and categorize it, so every ticket arrives at your team already rewritten and categorized.


Then a Router sends it down one of two branches, or an Otherwise path, to three Slack message steps.


Once the trigger is selected, its panel shows a connection field and a button to load sample data. Swap the trigger for a Notion event and the structure holds, so you can test each step against real sample data before anything goes live.


What follows from that is a budgeting question: price the workflow tool separately, then compare it with the Notion tier you would otherwise buy for automation alone.
